subtype: Sharing a loss in class or family [Receiver]
passage: On Monday morning the class teacher walked in with red eyes. The children stopped talking. “I have sad news,” she said. “Ganesh Bhaiya, our school guard, died yesterday. I knew him for many years, so I am very sad, and some of you may feel sad too. It's okay to cry, and it's okay to feel nothing yet.” Deepika whispered, “Is Miss crying?” Arohi nodded and held her school bag in her lap. The teacher gave everyone a sheet of paper. “If you like, draw or write something for his family.” Arohi drew a small gate with a chair beside it. Deepika sat close and shared her red crayon.

qa.q: What did the teacher give everyone after telling them the news?
qa.a: The teacher gave everyone a sheet of paper.

qa.q: What might Arohi be feeling as she holds her school bag in her lap and draws a small gate with a chair?
qa.a: Arohi seems sad and thoughtful, remembering the guard at the gate, and holding the bag closer suggests she needs something steady.

qa.q: What did the teacher do that helped the children with their sadness?
qa.a: The teacher told them plainly what happened, said it is okay to cry or to feel nothing yet, and gave them a quiet task to remember the guard.

qa.q: How might the teacher have felt while telling the class?
qa.a: The teacher was probably sad and trying to stay calm for the children, since the teacher knew the guard for many years and arrived with red eyes.

grounding: A child sees adults grieving at a death at school and is included in simple, honest ways.

subtype: Sharing a loss in class or family [Receiver]
passage: I'm Chandrika, ten, and I live in the flat below Mehak. On Sunday her Dada died, and by evening the upstairs flat was full of people crying and cooking. I saw Mehak's aunt try to send her out to play. Mehak stood at the door of the room where everyone sat and said, “Why can't I come in?” Her aunt looked at her for a moment, then made space on the sofa. “You can sit here,” she said. “Dada is gone, and everybody is sad. You can be sad too.” Mehak sat very still, holding a corner of her aunt's dupatta. I can't tell what she felt inside, but she did not ask to go and play.

qa.q: Where did Mehak's aunt make space for her?
qa.a: Mehak's aunt made space on the sofa.

qa.q: Why might Mehak have asked, “Why can't I come in?”
qa.a: Mehak seems to feel left out and wants to be with the family in what is happening, even without understanding it fully. 🤍

qa.q: What did the aunt do that helped Mehak?
qa.a: The aunt let Mehak in, said plainly that Dada is gone and everybody is sad, and said that Mehak could be sad too.

qa.q: What might it have been like for Mehak's aunt when Mehak asked to come in?
qa.a: The aunt may have felt torn between shielding Mehak and including her; the pause before making space on the sofa suggests the aunt chose to be honest.

grounding: A child sees adults crying at a death in the family and is included in a simple, honest way, seen by a child living downstairs.

subtype: Sharing a loss in class or family [Receiver]
passage: When Emil's grandmother died, the flat in Copenhagen filled with relatives he barely knew. His father cried at the kitchen table, which Emil had never seen before, and Emil hid behind the door. Aunt Lise found him there. She didn't send him to his room. 'Your farmor died last night. We're all very sad. It's okay to see Papa cry.' Then she asked if he wanted to help. Emil folded napkins for the memorial coffee and put a drawing of farmor's cat into the box going to the church. At school, his friend Bao gave him half of his lunch without saying anything. At the memorial, when everyone sang, Emil held his father's hand and sang the words he knew.

qa.q: What did Emil put into the box going to the church?
qa.a: A drawing of farmor's cat.

qa.q: Why might Emil have hidden behind the door?
qa.a: He was probably frightened and confused, never having seen his father cry before.

qa.q: What did Aunt Lise get right in how she helped Emil?
qa.a: She told him the truth simply, said it was okay to see Papa cry, and gave him small tasks so he could take part.

qa.q: How might Emil's father feel when Emil holds his hand at the memorial?
qa.a: He likely feels comforted and less alone in his grief, sharing the moment with his son.

grounding: A child sees adults grieve a death in the family and is helped by being included honestly and simply.

subtype: Sharing a loss in class or family [Receiver]
passage: On Monday morning, the principal came into Class 5B instead of Mr Pinto. She spoke slowly. 'Children, Mr Pinto died on Saturday. He had been ill for some time. It's all right to feel sad or confused.' Madhuri saw Mrs Sen at the door, wiping her eyes, and suddenly her own throat felt tight. Mehak began crying loudly. A boy at the back laughed nervously and then stopped. The principal didn't scold anyone. She let the class make cards for Mr Pinto's family and write one thing they remembered. Madhuri wrote about how he always said 'Good morning, scientists.' At lunch, she and Mehak sat together in the garden he had planted with them, not saying much.

qa.q: What did Mr Pinto always say to the class?
qa.a: 'Good morning, scientists.'

qa.q: What did Madhuri feel when she saw Mrs Sen wiping her eyes?
qa.a: Madhuri felt a rush of sadness, her throat tight, as if the adult's tears made it all right to feel it.

qa.q: How did the principal help the class grieve?
qa.a: She told them honestly, said sad or confused feelings were all right, didn't scold anyone, and let them make cards and share memories.

qa.q: What might the boy who laughed nervously have been feeling?
qa.a: He was likely awkward and overwhelmed rather than unkind; nervous laughter can come from shock.

grounding: Children see adults cry at a teacher's death and are helped by honest words and simple ways to take part.

subtype: Sharing a loss in class or family [Receiver]
passage: Tuesday: Nani died in the night. The grown-ups sent Nandini and her cousin Irawati next door 'to play'. Through the wall they heard crying. Nandini couldn't eat the neighbour aunty's poha; her stomach hurt from not knowing. Wednesday: at home, Mummy's eyes were swollen, and every time Nandini walked in, the adults stopped talking. Nandini began to wonder if she had done something wrong. Friday: Masi sat both girls down. 'Nani died because her heart was very old and tired. We're sad, and we're crying because we loved her. You can cry too, or ask anything.' Then she let them string marigolds for Nani's photo. Irawati asked if Nani could still hear them. Nandini finally cried, with Masi's arm around her.

qa.q: What did the girls string for Nani's photo?
qa.a: Marigolds.

qa.q: What was Nandini feeling on Wednesday?
qa.a: She felt anxious and confused, even worried she had done something wrong, because the adults stopped talking when she came in.

qa.q: Which of Masi's steps helped most, and why?
qa.a: Explaining simply and honestly why Nani died and inviting the girls to string marigolds, which ended the guessing and let them take part.

qa.q: How might Irawati be experiencing that week?
qa.a: Irawati was sent away too and is still trying to understand, as her question about whether Nani can hear them shows.

grounding: Over several days a child shielded from a family death feels confused, then is helped by simple, honest inclusion.

subtype: Sharing a loss in class or family [Receiver]
passage: Trisha, you asked why I let you come to Rukmini Aunty's prayer meeting. Let your Manoj Nana tell you about when I was eight. My Dadi died one winter, and the whole house changed overnight. My father, who never cried, sat on the floor with his head on his knees. My aunts wept in the kitchen. And everyone kept sending me outside to play. "He's too small," they said. I wasn't too small. I knew. I sat on the front steps and felt like the only one in the house without a job. Then my mother came out, took my hand and said, "Come, help me put flowers near her photo. Dadi liked marigolds." I cried then, properly, with all of them. So yes, beta, you come. You'll see us cry, and that is allowed.

qa.q: What flowers did Dadi like?
qa.a: Dadi liked marigolds.

qa.q: How did young Manoj feel while sitting on the front steps?
qa.a: He felt shut out and lonely, like the only one without a job in a grieving house, even though he understood what had happened.

qa.q: What choice inside the story helped young Manoj, and why?
qa.a: His mother included him by asking him to put flowers near Dadi's photo, which gave him an honest part in the grief and let him cry with the family.

qa.q: Why might the adults have kept sending Manoj outside to play?
qa.a: They probably wanted to shield a small child from their crying, not realising that being sent away made him feel more alone.

grounding: Manoj Nana recalls seeing adults grieve as a child, and how being included simply and honestly helped more than being shielded.
